terms.definition: A change in behavior as a result of experience. In aviation instruction it means the student can perform, decide, or explain something they could not before.
Learning theory that emphasizes observable behavior shaped by stimuli and reinforcement (rewards/consequences).
Learning theory focused on how the mind processes, stores, and retrieves information — thinking, memory, and problem solving.
View that learners build (construct) knowledge by connecting new information to what they already know and by active experience.
Lowest level of learning: ability to repeat back facts or steps without understanding why they matter.
Level of learning where the student comprehends meaning and relationships — can explain ideas in their own words.
Level of learning where the student can use knowledge or a skill correctly in a practical situation.
Highest level of learning: associating what was learned with other topics or new situations; judgment and transfer.
People learn best when they are ready (physically, mentally, emotionally) and when they see a reason to learn.
Things most often repeated are best remembered; practice strengthens learning, lack of practice weakens it.
Learning is strengthened when accompanied by a pleasant or satisfying feeling; weakened by frustration or punishment that is poorly applied.
Things learned first create a strong impression; teaching correctly the first time matters because unlearning bad habits is hard.
A vivid, exciting, or dramatic learning experience is remembered better than a routine or boring one.
Things most recently learned are best remembered; frequent review keeps skills sharp.
Knowledge domain of learning — remembering, understanding, applying, analyzing, evaluating, creating (thinking skills).
Attitudes, beliefs, values, and feelings — including motivation, professionalism, and safety culture.
Physical or motor skills — coordination, timing, and hands-on performance (e.g., flight maneuvers).
Very brief storage of raw sensory input (sights/sounds) before attention selects what enters short-term memory.
Limited-capacity, temporary holding area for information being used right now; needs rehearsal or encoding to last.
Relatively permanent store of knowledge and skills; retrieval depends on how well material was organized and linked.
Loss of ability to retrieve learned material — often from disuse, interference, or weak original encoding.
Applying knowledge or skill learned in one context to another. Positive transfer helps; negative transfer interferes.
Through correct practice, responses become automatic so attention can shift to higher-level decisions.
The reason a student engages and persists. Instructors foster motivation with clear goals, relevance, and success experiences.
Subconscious ways people protect self-image when stressed (e.g., rationalization, denial, projection, resignation).
Feeling of worry or unease that can help or hurt learning; mild anxiety may improve focus, excessive anxiety blocks performance.
A typical response to stress in training — e.g., nervousness, mild anxiety, or heightened alertness that still lets the student listen, learn, and perform safely.
A stress response that goes beyond normal nerves and impairs learning or safety — e.g., extreme fear, anger, or withdrawal. Instructors must recognize and manage these carefully.
Instructor-centered oral presentation of information; efficient for facts but limited for skill practice without follow-up activity.
Instructor leads students through questions so they discover or articulate ideas; builds understanding and involvement.
Instructor shows the skill, student practices with coaching — core method for psychomotor flight training.
Common pattern: explain, demonstrate, student performs, then critique/review to reinforce correct technique.
Teaching the student from early on to use outside visual references and flight instruments together, so instrument habits support (not replace) see-and-avoid flying.
Technology-supported instruction; useful for knowledge, scenario practice, and self-paced review when integrated into a lesson plan.
Device or material that supports a teaching point (chart, model, video, mockup). Chosen because it clarifies — not as decoration.
Organized outline of objectives, content, schedule, materials, and evaluation for a period of instruction.
Organized program of lessons leading to a certificate, rating, or defined competency.
Structured outline of blocks/stages of training, including content sequence and standards.
Training built around realistic scenarios so students practice decision-making, not only isolated maneuvers.
Constructive analysis of student performance after an activity; should be objective, flexible, acceptable, comprehensive, constructive, organized, thoughtful, and specific.
Measuring student progress against objectives — oral questions, written tests, performance checks, and practical tests.
Evaluation in a realistic context that mirrors how the skill or knowledge will be used (e.g., scenario oral, flight check).
Typical quizzes/tests that sample knowledge; useful but may not fully capture applied judgment.

terms.term: Characteristics of a good written test
terms.definition: Reliability, validity, comprehensiveness, discrimination, objectivity, and usability (practical to give and score).
Instructor conduct reflecting sincerity, acceptance of the student, personal appearance, and high standards of safety and ethics.
Help students learn; provide adequate instruction; demand standards; emphasize the positive; ensure student ability / end-of-course readiness; minimize barriers.
Motivate, keep students informed, approach as individuals, give credit when due, criticize constructively, be consistent, admit errors.
Factors that block progress — e.g., worry, lack of interest, physical discomfort, apathy, impatience, or inadequate instruction.
How a person sees themselves — abilities, worth, and identity. It filters perceptions: a confident self-concept helps a student accept instruction; a threatened one can block learning.
Meaning given to sensations; basis of all learning. Influenced by self-concept, goals, fear, and past experience.
Grouping perceptions into meaningful wholes — the “aha” when relationships suddenly make sense.
Patterns instructors must recognize and correct (e.g., anti-authority, impulsivity, invulnerability, macho, resignation).
